items.title: Measure 26-267 — Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of city's annual discretionary budget.
items.official_ballot_caption: Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of city's annual discretionary budget.
items.official_ballot_text: Measure No: 26-267 Caption: Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of city's annual discretionary budget. Question:  Should Portland create participatory budgeting program for residents to make binding decisions to spend 2% of city’s discretionary budget? Summary: Currently, Mayor works with City Administrator, bureaus, and community to develop proposed budget; Council then considers, amends as needed and adopts following public hearings. If measure is not approved, this process would not change. If measure approved, amended Charter would require Council to allocate an amount equivalent to at least 2% of the city’s adopted General Fund discretionary ongoing expenses (Council may identify funding from entire city budget to meet funding obligation) towards a participatory budgeting program that is: •       Developed with input from oversight committee, selected by a process determined by Council, of residents from all Council districts •      Open to any resident’s funding proposals for citywide or district projects: o       Proposals assessed and refined into limited number of feasible projects by city staff and budget delegates from all districts in a transparent process o        Feasible projects advance to binding selection process open, accessible to all residents •       Operational July 2027 •       Under recent forecast, preliminary estimate: o       16.4 million in FY 2027-28 o       17.0 million in FY 2028-29 •       Compliant with Oregon Local Budget Law Other provisions.
items.scope_note: Only appears for registered voters in the applicable local district; check your personal ballot.
items.independent_review_status: SOURCE_TEXT_INTERPRETED; OUTSIDE FINANCIAL AUDIT NOT COMPLETED

measure_brief.description: Would amend the Portland Charter to require a participatory budgeting program in which residents propose and select eligible city projects, with a recurring funding floor tied to city discretionary operating expenses.
measure_brief.yes: Require Portland to establish the resident-participatory process and allocate an amount equivalent to at least 2% of adopted General Fund discretionary ongoing expenses to it, with implementation starting in July 2027.
measure_brief.no: The proposed Charter requirement would not be enacted. Existing mayor, administration, council and public-hearing budget processes would continue unless changed by other action.
measure_brief.money: The ballot summary estimates $16.4 million in FY 2027–28 and $17.0 million in FY 2028–29. These are preliminary allocations under a 2% funding-floor formula, not guaranteed new taxes.
measure_brief.nuance: The 2% refers to an identified General Fund discretionary-ongoing expense base, not simply 2% of every city expenditure; the text says Council may draw from the overall city budget to satisfy the funding obligation. Resident proposals must still pass feasibility review before binding selection.
measure_brief.tradeoff_for: A continuing resident voice over funded projects rather than advice with no guaranteed funding.
measure_brief.tradeoff_against: A formula-based funding commitment can constrain later budget flexibility and requires administration; its benefit compared with a pilot has not been established.
measure_brief.unresolved: Exact implementation costs, approved project criteria, tradeoffs with other programs and final spending depend on subsequent Council decisions. No independent budget reconstruction completed.

voter_arguments.attribution: Published pamphlet statements and government explanatory text; statements are NOT verified facts.
voter_arguments.in_favor_or_official_rationale: Supporters argue that residents should make binding choices about a portion of city spending and point to neighborhood projects chosen through participatory budgeting elsewhere.
voter_arguments.opposition_or_concerns: Opponents argue that a recurring Charter-mandated amount, without a dedicated new revenue source, would compete with existing services and make the city budget less flexible.
voter_arguments.unverified: Advocacy claims about other cities, layoffs, cost-effectiveness and which city services would actually be cut are not independently verified here.

items.title: Measure 26-265 — Five-year Local Option Levy for Police, Fire & 911 Operations.
items.official_ballot_caption: Five-year Local Option Levy for Police, Fire & 911 Operations.
items.official_ballot_text: Measure No: 26-265 Caption: Five-year Local Option Levy for Police, Fire & 911 Operations. Question:  Shall Troutdale adopt a local option levy at $1.60 per $1,000 of assessed value for police, fire & 911 services? This measure may cause property taxes to increase more than three percent. Summary: Troutdale provides Police, Fire, and 911 through contracts: Multnomah County Sheriff's Office, City of Gresham Fire Department, and Bureau of Emergency Communications. Costs of essential public safety services continually increase and are projected to rise faster than available funding. Without a sustainable funding source, the gap between revenues and public safety costs will become unsustainable, risking the long-term reliability of Police, Fire, and 911 services. If this measure passes, the current Council will replace the $25 Public Safety Fee, with a voter-approved local option levy of $1.60 per $1,000 of assessed property value. The average Troutdale home assessed at approximately $267,800, would cost about $428.48 annually. Because the Public Safety Utility Fee would be eliminated, the average homeowner would not pay the current $300 annual fee, resulting in an estimated net annual cost increase of approximately $128.48 while providing dedicated funding for Police, Fire, and 911 services. The amount collected is estimated to be $3,556,392 in 2027-28, $3,663,084 in 2028-29, $3,772,977 in 2029-30, $3,886,166 in 2030-31, and $4,002,751 in 2031-32. Public safety costs already exceed $10 million annually and are projected to surpass $14 million by 2030. This levy ensures stable, reliable public safety funding for Troutdale’s future.

measure_brief.description: Troutdale would adopt a five-year $1.60-per-$1,000 assessed-value local-option levy for contracted police, fire and 911 operations.
measure_brief.yes: Authorize the levy. The city states that the current Council would replace a $25-per-month Public Safety Utility Fee with the levy; check enactment and future Council decisions separately.
measure_brief.no: Do not authorize this new local-option levy; existing contracts, fees and future budget decisions remain separate questions. A no vote does not itself reduce contracted service costs.
measure_brief.money: At the city’s $267,800 example assessed value, the levy is $428.48 per year. The cited replacement of a $300 annual fee yields an estimated $128.48 net increase for that example, conditional on fee elimination.
measure_brief.nuance: Compare the net change after the planned fee replacement, not just gross tax cost. Assessed value differs from market value; the actual bill depends on the parcel and tax rules.
measure_brief.tradeoff_for: Dedicated revenue to fund rising costs of contracted public-safety and dispatch services.
measure_brief.tradeoff_against: Higher net household costs for the example property; the levy itself does not prove costs are being managed efficiently or guarantee service outcomes.
measure_brief.unresolved: Independent review of contract costs, staffing/service alternatives and parcel-level tax impacts has not been completed.

voter_arguments.attribution: Published pamphlet statements and government explanatory text; statements are NOT verified facts.
voter_arguments.in_favor_or_official_rationale: The city’s explanatory statement projects a growing gap between contracted police, fire and 911 costs and available revenue, and proposes dedicated temporary levy funding as one response. This is the city’s explanation, not a submitted pro argument.
voter_arguments.opposition_or_concerns: A published opposition argument says the city should finish contract restructuring and long-term service planning before raising a temporary levy. It cites a potential savings projection that has not been independently replicated.
voter_arguments.unverified: Neither the city’s cost trajectory nor the opposition’s projected $8.1 million savings has been independently reconstructed.

items.title: Measure 26-266 — ADVISORY VOTE: Should Troutdale Create a Municipal Police Department?
items.official_ballot_caption: ADVISORY VOTE: Should Troutdale Create a Municipal Police Department?
items.official_ballot_text: Measure No: 26-266 Caption: ADVISORY VOTE: Should Troutdale Create a Municipal Police Department? Question:  ADVISORY VOTE: Should the City proceed with planning and creation of a Troutdale Police Department? Summary: This is a non-binding advisory vote and does not authorize or impose any tax, fee, or expenditure. This is a non-binding advisory vote and does not authorize or impose any tax, fee, or expenditure. In 2015, the City of Troutdale dissolved its Police Department and contracted with the Multnomah County Sheriff's Office to provide police services. The decision was based, in part, on the expectation that contracting would reduce long-term costs while maintaining public safety services. Since then, the cost of contracted police services has increased, and the City has continued evaluating service levels, operational needs, community expectations, and long-term financial sustainability. As part of that review, the City has developed preliminary plans for the possible re-establishment of a Troutdale Police Department. This advisory vote asks whether the City should continue planning to create a Troutdale Police Department while evaluating the costs, operational considerations, and benefits of both a municipal Police Department and continued contracted police services. The City Council will consider the results of this advisory vote when evaluating future police service options.

measure_brief.yes: Signal support for further planning and examination of creating a municipal police department; does not establish or fund one.

items.title: Measure 34-355 — Bonds Fixing Failing & Aging Infrastructure; Improving Safety, Vocational Facilities.

items.official_ballot_text: Measure No: 34-355 Caption: Bonds Fixing Failing & Aging Infrastructure; Improving Safety, Vocational Facilities. Question:  Shall District issue bonds to increase safety, security, repair aging schools and failing infrastructure, expand vocational classrooms, secure matching funds? If the bonds are approved, they will be payable from taxes on property or property ownership that are not subject to the limits of sections 11 and 11b, Article XI of the Oregon Constitution. Measure No: 34-355 Summary:                Lower Tax Rate: This measure is expected to result in a bond levy rate of $1.84 per $1,000 assessed value - lower than the average rate paid since last bond approval. If passed, District is eligible for $6.1 million in state matching funds. Hillsboro School District seeks approval for a principal amount of $430 million in general obligation bonds to finance capital costs, including: Fix Aging Buildings: Replace failing roofs, siding, HVAC, plumbing, flooring, and lighting. Healthy Schools: Replace systems causing leaks, mold, closed classrooms Safety & Security: New doors, locks, fencing, cameras, phone systems, building automation. Enhance cybersecurity, network infrastructure. Career & Technical Education: Update computing labs, create fire science classroom, expand STEM and vocational spaces. Additional Projects: Field, track, and Title IX upgrades; bus, kitchen, fleet and aging technology replacements. Requires community oversight committee, regular audits. Financials: o  Bonds may be issued in multiple series, each maturing within 21 years from issuance. o  Estimated levy rate is $1.84 per $1,000 of assessed value. o   Actual levy rates may differ due to interest rates, changes in property value

measure_brief.yes: Authorize the district to issue the described general-obligation bonds for eligible capital projects, with separate oversight and issuance decisions.

items.title: Measure 26-268 — Bonds to Increase Safety, Security; Repair, Construct Schools; Increase Accessibility
items.official_ballot_caption: Bonds to Increase Safety, Security; Repair, Construct Schools; Increase Accessibility
items.official_ballot_text: Measure No: 26-268 Caption: Bonds to Increase Safety, Security; Repair, Construct Schools; Increase Accessibility Question:  Shall District issue bonds, projected to maintain 2026 bond rate, to increase safety, repair, replace aging schools and increase accessibility? If the bonds are approved, they will be payable from taxes on property or property ownership that are not subject to the limits of sections 11 and 11b, Article XI of the Oregon Constitution. Summary: This measure is projected to maintain District's 2026 bond levy rate of $1.62/$1,000 of assessed value. If passed, District will receive $8,168,000 in state matching funds. Reynolds School District seeks approval for a principal amount of $162.5 million in bonds to finance capital costs, including: Replace Aging Glenfair Elementary: Replace the 72-year-old school, which is overcrowded, has building systems beyond repair, contains hazardous materials, and has outdated safety & security measures. Replacement estimated to cost less than renovation. Repair Failing Infrastructure: •        Roofing, HVAC, plumbing, electrical systems, water heater replacement districtwide. Safety & Security: •      New fire alarm systems, PA systems, perimeter security across the district. Accessibility: •      ADA upgrades including accessible parking, sidewalks, ramps districtwide. Additional Projects: •      New turf field, bleachers at Reynolds High School. Requires community oversight committee, regular audits. Financials: •      Bonds may be issued in multiple series, each maturing within 21 years from issuance. •      No increase to 2026 bond levy rate of $1.62 per $1,000 of assessed value expected. •        Actual bond levy rate may differ due to interest rates, changes in property value.

measure_brief.description: Reynolds School District proposes $162.5 million in bond principal for replacing Glenfair Elementary, districtwide repairs, safety and accessibility.
measure_brief.yes: Authorize the district to issue the described bonds for eligible capital improvements, subject to actual project and issuance decisions.
measure_brief.no: Do not authorize these bonds; building and maintenance requirements remain, and existing funding is unaffected by the ballot choice.
measure_brief.money: $162.5 million principal. The ballot forecasts a $1.62-per-$1,000 assessed-value bond rate, approximately unchanged from 2026, and $8.168 million in conditional state matching funds.
measure_brief.nuance: “No rate increase expected” is a forecast for the bond levy, not a promise that no household’s total bill changes. Bond capital funds are not general school operating funds.
measure_brief.tradeoff_for: Addresses school replacement, safety and accessibility needs and could obtain state matching funds.
measure_brief.tradeoff_against: Commits future property-tax revenues for bond repayment and interest; comparative renovation alternatives need scrutiny.
measure_brief.unresolved: Independent facility-condition verification, construction costs and repayment modeling remain incomplete.

voter_arguments.attribution: Published pamphlet statements and government explanatory text; statements are NOT verified facts.

voter_arguments.unverified: The claimed zero rate increase is a forecast for the bond levy, not a guarantee that every property’s bill will remain unchanged.

items.title: Measure 26-269 — Five-Year Local Option Tax for Fire & Ambulance Operations
items.official_ballot_caption: Five-Year Local Option Tax for Fire & Ambulance Operations
items.official_ballot_text: Measure No: 26-269 Caption: Five-Year Local Option Tax for Fire & Ambulance Operations Question:  Question: Shall the District create a new five-year levy of $1.70 per $1000 of assessed value for five years beginning 2027-2028? This measure creates new local option taxes which may cause property taxes to increase more than three percent. Summary: Summary: The taxes will be used to meet the expenses Burlington Water District pays for emergency services (Fire and Ambulance)and to maintain a contingency fund for the future increased expenses. An estimate of the total amount to be raised each fiscal year is: $84,420 in 2027-2028 $86,953 in 2028-2029 $89,561 In 2029-2030 $92,248 In 2030-2031 $95,016 in 2031-2032 The estimated tax cost for this measure is an ESTIMATE ONLY based on the best information available from the county assessor at the time of the estimate and may reflect the impact of early payment discounts, compression and the collection rate. A property with an assessed value of $166,000.00, the average assessed value for the district, will pay an estimated $24 per month in additional property taxes.

items.independent_review_status: SOURCE_TEXT_INTERPRETED; OUTSIDE FINANCIAL AUDIT NOT COMPLETED

measure_brief.description: Burlington Water District proposes a five-year local-option property tax for fire and ambulance operating expenses and a contingency reserve.
measure_brief.yes: Authorize the stated $1.70-per-$1,000 assessed-value levy for five fiscal years beginning 2027–28.
measure_brief.no: Do not authorize the new levy; the district would need other budget decisions or resources to fund the stated service obligations.
measure_brief.money: At the ballot’s $166,000 assessed-value example, 1.70 × 166 = $282.20 annually (about $23.52 per month), consistent with the approximate $24/month cited in the official summary.
measure_brief.nuance: The question calls this a new tax, not a continuation of an existing levy. Verify which district properties are covered; this measure is not on every Multnomah ballot.
measure_brief.tradeoff_for: Provides earmarked funds for specified emergency-service obligations and a contingency reserve.
measure_brief.tradeoff_against: Imposes a new five-year property-tax cost, while the details of contracts and alternatives still need confirmation.
measure_brief.unresolved: Independently audited fire/ambulance expense history, contracts, alternative funding and full parcel-level impacts are not available in this pass.

voter_arguments.attribution: Published pamphlet statements and government explanatory text; statements are NOT verified facts.
